newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Swedish '97 budget rules out spending cuts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Swedish '97 budget rules out spending cuts.

text.p: Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink on Friday presented a confident 1997 budget, pledging a budget surplus by 1998 without further spending cuts and compliance with Maastricht Treaty currency union requirements.

In his first full budget since taking over the finance ministry from Prime Minister Goran Persson in March, Asbrink said the recovery in state finances had been quicker than the government tipped in its spring budget, which contained swinging public spending cuts.
This, combined with economic recovery in Sweden and abroad, ruled out the need for further cuts, he said.

"The strengthening of the Swedish economy has progressed more quickly than the government expected. Thus, the budget bill contains no new proposals for savings other than specification of the (existing) 126 billion crown programme," he said.

Even though Asbrink's no-surprise budget was devoid of spending cuts, a combination of low inflation, strong exports and appreciation in the Swedish currency would mean balance in the budget by 1998 and a "permanent surplus" thereafter.

The Social Democratic government reaffirmed its belief that full-scale economic recovery was just around the corner, although the main economic scenario presented in the budget promised little in the way of economic growth.
Gross domestic product growth was seen at just 1.6 percent this year, rising to 2.3 percent in 1997 and peaking at 2.6 percent in 1998.
This will do little to help Persson achieve his central aim of cutting unemployment to four percent by the end of the century from current levels of 8.8 percent.
However, the tone of the budget was otherwise optimistic.

Sweden's budget deficit expressed as a percentage of GDP was seen falling to just four percent this year and 2.6 percent in 1997, bringing the country well within the three percent Maastricht requirement for monetary union under the third phase of the European Union's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Although Sweden will strive to conform with the Maastricht demands, Asbrink flagged a collision course with central bank governor Urban Backstrom on the subject of Swedish membership of Europe's existing Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).

"In the government's opinion, participation in the European Exchange Rate Mechanism, is not on the agenda," the budget document said, expressing a far more hawkish stance on currency union than the Riksbank governor.

Backstrom said on Thursday it was time to begin discussing Swedish ERM membership, although he emphasised that the Riksbank -- which makes the final decision on membership -- was not in the process of making a firm decision.
Economists gave a guarded welcome to the 1997 budget, the first full budget to utilise a state spending cap system introduced in April.
Carl B. Hamilton, chief economist at Sweden's Handelsbanken, said Asbrink's assumptions were extremely vulnerable to swings in the business cycle.

"Public finances are very sensitive to business fluctuations, so if we have a downturn in a few years' time we are uncertain how the budget deficit will behave...but for the next two years the situation looks promising," Hamilton said.
